title: Web Development Basics: Just the Essentials

intro.text: You've been handing work to Claude Code without really knowing what it's producing — which means you can't yet tell good work from sloppy work. This chapter fixes that — just enough. You'll learn how the web actually works, then meet the three languages every web page is built from: HTML for layout, CSS for style, and JavaScript for behavior. Then you'll direct the AI through your first real mini-project — a pomodoro timer — reviewing its output at every step, and have it pushed to the cloud so anyone on the internet can use it.

intro.title: Before you continue
intro.text: This chapter teaches just the essentials — enough HTML and CSS to review and fine-tune what AI writes for you, and enough JavaScript to read AI-generated code. You are not training to hand-write everything; you're training to be a good reviewer.

lessons.title: The Internet and the Web
lessons.objective: Understand what the web is and how it works under the hood — well enough to follow what your AI is building in the upcoming HTML, CSS, and JavaScript lessons, and to ask the right questions about it.

blocks.text: When you type youtube.com into your browser's address bar and press Enter, the following things happen in order:
Your browser sends the site's server a request: “Please send me the information I need to draw this page.”
The server sends back a text file that describes the page.
The browser reads that text file line by line and draws the screen (this process is called rendering).
“If you want an analogy: a web page is a recipe, and the browser is the chef who cooks from that recipe.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

steps.title: The three languages that describe a web page

blocks.text: Plain English is too fuzzy to describe a page's structure precisely, so the web uses three programming languages together. Everything your AI produces for a web page will be written in one of these — so knowing which language owns which job tells you where to look when something's off:
HTML: describes which elements go on the page and how they're laid out.
CSS: decides each element's style — color, size, spacing, and so on.
JavaScript: describes behavior and features that react to the user — like what happens when a button is clicked.

steps.title: Why learn the basics at all?

blocks.text: Even when AI writes all the code, a manager needs a minimum of language knowledge to review the result and fine-tune it to what you actually wanted. Without it, you're approving work you can't judge. The good news: HTML and CSS have simple rules you can pick up fast, and we'll only cover JavaScript to the level where you can read and review code the AI wrote.

lessons.title: Laying Out a Page with HTML
lessons.objective: Understand how HTML lays out the elements of a web page, the basic unit called a tag, and the standard structure of an HTML document — well enough to open any HTML file the AI produces and spot when the skeleton is wrong.

blocks.text: HTML is a text file made up of tags.
A tag is a piece of syntax wrapped in angle brackets (<>) that labels what an element of the page is — text, an image, a link, and so on.

A human can glance at a printed page and instantly tell the hierarchy from big type and small type. A browser has no such intuition — so each piece of text has to be labeled: “this one's a heading, that one's a paragraph.” When you review AI-written HTML, you're checking that it applied those labels the way you intended.

rows: An ordinary paragraph of body text

blocks.text:
There's a designated tag for everything you might want to express. Headings are

(short for heading), paragraph text is

(short for paragraph), images are , links are (for anchor), and so on.

The very same text — “Alex Carter” — looks completely different depending on which tag holds it. Put it in

and it renders as a huge heading; put it in

and it's one ordinary line of body text.
“A tag is a label that tells the browser what this text is.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

blocks.text: HTML is a bundle of tags wrapped in angle brackets (<>), and they follow a few simple rules:
The text inside the brackets determines the tag's name. Example: <h1> is an h1 tag.
As a rule, every tag comes as a pair: an opening tag and a closing tag.
The closing tag has a slash (/) in front of the name.

Alex Carter

│ │ └─ closing tag — the / means “this ends here” │ └─ content of the tag └─ opening tag — “h1” is the tag name
blocks.label: Reference example

blocks.text:
The text between the opening tag and the closing tag is that tag's content. In the examples above, “Alex Carter” is the content of the

, and “Hello there” is the content of the

.

blocks.title: Before you continue
blocks.text:
Some tags finish in a single stroke, with no closing tag at all (for example and
). We'll cover those in the next lesson.
Start with the two most basic tags — the ones that show up directly on screen:
<h1> – <h6>: headings. The smaller the number, the bigger the heading — h1 is the largest and h6 the smallest.
: an ordinary paragraph of text.

h1 usually appears only once per page, and the hierarchy builds downward through h2 and h3. A well-planned heading hierarchy doubles as the page's table of contents — and it's one of the first things to check in AI-generated pages.

steps.title: Structure tags you don't see on screen

blocks.text: Open any HTML file and you'll find tags that never show up on screen but are absolutely required. They're the ones responsible for the page's skeleton:
<!DOCTYPE html>: tells the browser this file is an HTML document.
<html>: the top-level frame that wraps every other HTML tag.
<head>: the area that holds settings about the page itself. The <title> inside it sets the page title shown on the browser tab.
<body>: the area that holds everything actually visible on screen. Content tags like h1 and p all go inside here.
Put those four together and the simplest possible HTML file usually looks like this:

Alex Carter

Hello there
blocks.label: Reference example

blocks.text: The structure is: head and body sit side by side inside html, and every content tag gathers under body.

lessons.title: HTML's Essential Tags
lessons.objective: Continue from the last lesson with the core HTML tags used most in practice, and learn the concepts of attributes and self-closing tags — so you can read AI-generated HTML and confirm each element is the right kind.

steps.title: A tour of the essential tags

blocks.text: <h1> – <h6>: headings, level 1 through 6. In practice you'll see down to about h2 most often.
: displays an image. The src attribute specifies the image's path.
<input>: a form element that accepts user input — text, numbers, and so on.
<button>: a clickable button.
<div>: a region container for grouping elements that share a style.
<a>: a link that navigates to another page. The href attribute specifies the destination address.
Google about page
blocks.label: Reference example

blocks.text: The extras that follow a tag name — src, href, class, and friends — are attributes. They fine-tune how the tag behaves. When a link goes nowhere or an image is broken, a wrong attribute value is usually the culprit.
A tag like has no text to hold inside, so instead of a separate closing tag it closes itself: a slash at the end of the opening tag. This is called self-closing.
└─ attribute, written as name="value" e.g. src tells the tag which image file path to point at
blocks.label: Reference example

lessons.title: Styling with CSS
lessons.objective: Understand what CSS is, how styles get applied to HTML elements, and the two most-used selectors — well enough to check that AI-written styles target the elements you actually meant.

blocks.alt: HTML supplies structure; CSS changes its appearance.
blocks.caption: HTML supplies structure; CSS changes its appearance.

blocks.text: The same HTML structure, before and after CSS: structure from HTML, looks from CSS.
Build a page's skeleton with HTML alone and the screen is just text, neatly stacked. The colors, the sizes, the spacing — everything is the browser's plain default.

Dressing that skeleton in visual style is CSS's job. Text color, backgrounds, spacing, alignment, fonts, shadows, even animation — pretty much every part of the screen you'd call “design” is CSS's responsibility. The exact same HTML can look completely different depending on which CSS is put on it — so when the AI's page looks wrong but behaves right, CSS is where to send it back for fixes.
“If HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the appearance.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

CSS code is written inside a <style> tag in the HTML (or in a separate .css file). One bundle of style rules is put together like this:

<style>
  body {                          ← selector
    background-color: lightblue;  ← property: value
    font-size: 16px;
  }
</style>
blocks.label: Reference example

blocks.text: The selector before the curly braces decides which elements this applies to, and inside the braces go property: value pairs, one per line. Don't forget the semicolon at the end of each line — it's required, and a missing one is a common reason a style silently fails to apply.
CSS has roughly 500 properties, but they're all plain English words, so the meaning is easy to guess. For example: font-size, margin, color, border-bottom.

steps.title: The two selectors you'll actually use

blocks.text: Tag selector
Write a tag's name as-is and the same style applies to every tag of that kind on the page:

h1 { color: navy; }
└─ selector = the tag name: every h1 on the page turns navy at once
blocks.label: Reference example

blocks.text: Class selector
Use this when you want to style only the specific elements you designate, regardless of tag type:
HTML — give the tag a name with the class attribute: Google CSS — a dot (.) plus the same name: .google-link { color: green; }
blocks.label: Reference example

blocks.text: In HTML you attach a class to a tag with class="name"; in CSS you select only the elements carrying that class by putting a dot in front of the same name: .name. Give the same class to several tags and they all get styled in one shot.
First give the HTML element a class="name" attribute, then select it in CSS as .name.
This is the selector used most in real-world work — expect to see it all over AI-generated CSS.
The Google link appears in index.html. Its class name matches the CSS selector.

blocks.text: Write all the CSS inside the <style> tag and the file gets long and hard to read. The usual practice — and what a well-organized AI should do — is to split it into a separate file like style.css and pull it in from the HTML's <head>.

lessons.title: Adding Behavior with JavaScript
lessons.objective: Understand what JavaScript is and how it adds behavior and features to HTML elements — functions, events, and the flow of modifying HTML elements from JavaScript — well enough to trace whether AI-written code actually wires a button to the action you asked for.

blocks.text: JavaScript is the language that gives behavior to the elements laid out with HTML and styled with CSS. An alert pops when a button is pressed, new elements get added or removed — the parts we casually call “features” are JavaScript's department. When a feature you requested doesn't fire, this is the file to question.
HTML and CSS build the screen; JavaScript makes that screen interact with the user.

blocks.title: Check the starting page
blocks.text: The next prompt refers to a Confirm button. If index.html does not yet contain a real button labeled Confirm, ask Claude to add that button first. Keep the Google link as a link. Then use the original prompt below.

blocks.text:

blocks.label: Claude Code prompt

blocks.text: Refresh index.html, enter text in the new input field, and click Confirm to check the requested behavior.
JavaScript code is written inside HTML's <script> tag — exactly the same pattern as writing CSS inside <style>:

<script>
  // your JavaScript code goes here
</script>
blocks.label: Reference example

blocks.text: The browser reads HTML from top to bottom, and the moment it meets a <script>, it runs the code inside.

A bundle of code that performs a specific job is called a function. It's the same idea as the word “meal” bundling a whole series of actions — putting food in your mouth, chewing, swallowing — into a single word.

blocks.label: Reference example

blocks.text: A function is declared starting with the function keyword, then the function's name with () after it. The code inside the curly braces is the function's body, and calling the name — like handleClick() — runs the whole body at once.
“A function is a named bundle of actions.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

steps.title: Event handlers: deciding when a function runs

blocks.text: Just creating a function makes nothing happen. The page also has to be told when to run it — and a function that exists but is never wired up is one of the most common gaps to catch in AI-written code.
Every single user action — clicking a button, hovering the mouse, pressing a key — is called an event. The thing that connects “when this event happens” to “run that function” is an event handler:

blocks.where: wiring a function to a click
blocks.label: Reference example

blocks.text: Attributes like onclick on an HTML tag are event handlers. The button above calls the handleClick() function when clicked — so pressing it pops the “Confirmed!” alert. Note that the handleClick name has to match in both places for the connection to work — a mismatch means a button that silently does nothing.
Beyond onclick there's a handler attribute ready for every kind of event: onmouseover (mouse hovers), onkeydown (key pressed), and many more.
JavaScript can also create brand-new HTML elements on a screen that's already drawn, change their contents, or delete them:
Read the value typed into an input form and add a new item to the screen.
Press a delete button and remove that element.
Every interaction on services like Instagram or X (Twitter) is built exactly this way.

steps.title: Why the time survives a refresh

blocks.text: No server, no database — yet the changed time sticks. The secret is a storage space the browser itself owns, called Local Storage. Knowing it exists lets you ask the right question when data should (or shouldn't) persist:
A small data store inside the browser. JavaScript can freely save and read key–value data in it.
Local Storage usually survives refreshes and browser restarts. It can be cleared by the user or browser, and private browsing has different persistence behavior.
But it's only reachable from that browser on that computer. Open the site on a different PC and the data isn't there. To share across devices you'd need a separate database.
Local Storage keeps small values in the current browser. It is not a shared online database.
Plenty of services lean on this space: temporarily saved shopping carts, personal preferences, and more. At the “little tool just for me” stage — like our pomodoro — local storage alone is plenty.

lessons.title: Deploying to the Cloud
lessons.objective: Understand how a web server delivers your website, then put your Pomodoro timer online with Netlify.

steps.title: From your laptop to a public link

blocks.text: Your Pomodoro timer currently opens from files on your own computer. Sending someone that folder path does not give them access to your copy.
Deployment means putting a copy of your website on a hosting service so people can visit it using a web address.

blocks.alt: Before deployment, your browser opens files on your laptop. After you upload them to Netlify, visitors use a web address to access the hosted copy.
blocks.caption: Deployment gives other people a place to visit your website.

steps.title: How web servers and Netlify work

blocks.text: What does a web server do?
A web server is software that receives a browser’s request and sends back the files or data it needs.

blocks.alt: 1. The visitor’s browser asks for your page. 2. The web server sends HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files. 3. The browser displays the page and runs the Pomodoro timer.
blocks.caption: For this timer, the server sends the files. The browser displays the page and runs the timer.

blocks.text: When a classmate opens your link, their browser asks for your page. The server sends the website files. Their browser uses those files to show and run your timer.

blocks.title: Does “server” mean a computer or a program?

blocks.text: You will hear both uses. A computer can be called a server, and the software running on it can also be called a server. Here, focus on its job: respond to the browser’s request.
What Netlify does for you
The cloud means using computers managed by a provider over the internet. Netlify is the hosting service we will use for this lesson.

rows: Hosts the website files and gives you a web address.
Loads the files and runs the timer.

blocks.text: You do not need to install a separate web server for this exercise. Visitors use the copy hosted by Netlify, so your laptop does not need to stay on.

blocks.title: If you change the timer later

blocks.text: Saving a change on your laptop does not update this manually uploaded site. Upload the updated project folder to the same Netlify project to publish the new version.

rows: Run the software so it can receive requests.
The server stopped unexpectedly. There can be many causes.
Update or repair the service. It may be briefly unavailable.

blocks.text: Deployment finishes and the project overview opens.

Check the visibility label near the project name. If it says Private, visitors outside your team cannot open the website. If the project is already public, continue to Open and test your public site below.

blocks.alt: Guidebook screenshot for Make the website public
blocks.caption: Make the website public

blocks.text: For a private project, click Make public.

blocks.alt: Guidebook screenshot for Make the website public
blocks.caption: Make the website public

blocks.text: In the dialog, you can edit the website name. If you change it, click the green check mark to confirm. Then click Make public at the bottom.

blocks.alt: Guidebook screenshot for Make the website public
blocks.caption: Make the website public

blocks.text: The site is public. Continue to Open and test your public site below.

blocks.title: Open and test your public site

blocks.text: When Netlify confirms that your project is public, open the displayed address. Check that the timer and settings page work.

blocks.alt: Guidebook screenshot for Open your website and find its address settings
blocks.caption: Open your website and find its address settings

blocks.text: To change the address later, open the project overview and click Go to Domain management. The next two steps show how to rename the default netlify.app address.

blocks.alt: Guidebook screenshot for Open your website and find its address settings
blocks.caption: Open your website and find its address settings

blocks.text: The public address opens your timer, and the timer and settings page work.

blocks.title: Rename the default address if you want to

blocks.text: Under Production domains, open Options next to the Netlify address and choose Edit project name.

blocks.alt: Guidebook screenshot for Change the default website address
blocks.caption: Change the default website address

blocks.text: Enter an available project name and click Save. Netlify updates the default address to your-project-name.netlify.app.

blocks.alt: Guidebook screenshot for Change the default website address
blocks.caption: Change the default website address

blocks.text: If you changed the name, Netlify displays the new default address.

blocks.title: Check the address you will share

blocks.text: Click Project overview in the left sidebar to return to your project.

blocks.alt: Guidebook screenshot for Check the updated address
blocks.caption: Check the updated address

blocks.text: Confirm that the new address appears, then open it to check your website. Use this updated address when sharing your project.

blocks.alt: Guidebook screenshot for Check the updated address
blocks.caption: Check the updated address

blocks.text: The address you plan to share opens the correct website.
